sweep_summary: Two title-keyword items for utes1238, neither openly available in full. (1) Harms 1966 (IJAL, DOI 10.1086/464907): paywalled; the 'open access' pointer Semantic Scholar/Unpaywall give is just a WALS bibliographic record. Using the public archive.org full-text-search API on the lending-restricted IJAL 32(3) scan I recovered the stress statement verbatim: 'Rule (6) accounts for the alternation of mora stress in Southern Paiute by which odd numbered vowels, counting from the initial vowel, are unstressed as long as one stressed vowel remains before the final vowel (which is unstressed and voiceless by rule (5))' — confirms the catalog's second-mora fixed-strict coding and adds the final-vowel-always-unstressed clause; the prose reading of even-length words is 0100 (McLaughlin's), but the formal derivations McLaughlin criticizes were not readable, so the 0110-vs-0100 cells stay open. Full text still high priority. (2) Oberly 2013 (Benjamins, DOI 10.1075/clu.8.04obe): closed; Crossref abstract obtained — an instrumental study of the correlates of Southern Ute stress (five speakers, 100 words, placement data from two speakers) but no placement statement; medium priority. Her 2008 Arizona dissertation (the fuller source) could not be reached (repository.arizona.edu 403 on every route; Bonus first-hand Ute witnesses surfaced by the same full-text search (snippets only, both lending-restricted on archive.org): Goss 1970 ('Voiceless Vowels (?) in Numic Languages', Liljeblad Festschrift) gives six numbered Southern Ute stress rules — odd syllables weak, even strong, final unstressed, penultimate always strong, primary on the first strong syllable, secondary on the last strong syllable — and Goss's linguistic note in Smith 1974 gives the same system for Northern Ute ('bisyllabic words... carry primary stress on the first syllable, and 2) all longer words carry primary stress on the second syllable'). Both reproduce the catalog's rule string 10 010 0110 01010 010110 (binary plus always-strong penult) for Ute, syllable- rather than mora-counting, and should be added as same-languoid support for the even-length clash cells and for the dialect caution. Nothing read supersedes Sapir 1930 §10 p. 39 as the deciding source. All fetched sources records and the consolidated snippet file are under ( written, stamped).

new_statements.locator: IJAL 32(3): 228-235, the sentence introducing Rule (6) in the stress section (page not recoverable from the archive.org full-text-search API; StressTyp2 cites p. 232 for the same passage). new_statements.reading: Stress alternates by mora from the left: odd vowels unstressed, even vowels stressed, so the second mora carries the main stress; the final vowel is always unstressed (and voiceless); the 'as long as one stressed vowel remains before the final vowel' clause gives disyllables initial stress. This confirms the catalog's fixed-strict, second-mora coding and the WORD domain. On the disputed even-length cells the prose reads as 0100 (no stressed penult) for four-mora words, agreeing with McLaughlin 1984 against the catalog's 0110 — but McLaughlin 1984:59 reports that Harms' formal rules leave the penult stressed, and the derivations are not in the readable snippets, so this item does not settle those cells. Not first-hand fieldwork (a restatement of Sapir's corpus); the first-hand statements read this sweep are Goss 1970 (Southern Ute) and Goss in Smith 1974 (Northern Ute), both snippet-only, whose syllable-counting rules with an always-strong penult reproduce the catalog's clash cells for Ute.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim on the held Sapir 1930 p. 39 page image and two held text layers. (2) Deciding source: Sapir 1930 is a 296-pp reference grammar and the best description of Southern Paiute proper; the 'fixed' (second-mora ~ second-syllable, initial in disyllables) classification and WORD domain are well-sourced, with the mora idealization already flagged (M11). (3) The risk is confined to the rule string's even-length cells (0110/010110/01010110, the 'binary+clash' profile that makes this the cell-46 language): Sapir prints no n>=4 penult secondary; the cells come from Hayes 1995:266 and Gordon 2002 plus an internal projection of Sapir's disyllabic retraction. McLaughlin 1984 (fetched sources and read now, pp. 50-51, 59, 75-76), working from Sapir's corpus and Franklin & Bunte's modern data, formalizes stress as even-numbered NON-FINAL vowels with initial stress only in disyllables

sources.quote: Following the phonetic tradition of Ladefoged and Maddieson, this chapter reports results of the first phonetic instrumental analysis of stress in Southern Ute, a severely endangered Uto-Aztecan language. The phonetic correlates of stress could include changes in duration, pitch and/or intensity (Ladefoged 2006). This analysis is based on a list of 100 words designed to determine the phonetic correlates of stress. Five speakers (three female and two male) were recorded using a frame sentence to control intonation. Stress placement data was elicited from one male and one female speaker.
sources.note: Only instrumental study of stress in any dialect of the utes1238 languoid (Southern Ute); checks whether second-mora primary and alternating secondaries survive acoustically; relevant because the record is keyed at language level though it describes Sapir's Kaibab Southern Paiute.

sources.quote: Stress is predictable in Ute. The final syllable of a Ute word is always weak stressed and devoiced, The penultimate Syllable is always strong. If the word is longer than two Syllables, counting from the initial syllable, every even Syllable is strong and every odd one is weak. The first [footnote intervenes] strong syllable of a word carries primary word stress. The result is: 1) bisyllabic words (the minimal free form in Ute) carry primary stress on the first syllable, and 2) all longer words carry primary stress on the second syllable.
sources.locator: Goss's linguistic note in Smith 1974 (page not recoverable from the snippet API)
sources.note: Northern Ute (Uintah-Ouray): same system as Goss 1970 for Southern Ute — even syllables strong counting from the left, penult always strong, final always weak and devoiced; primary stress on the first strong syllable, so initial in disyllables and second-syllable in all longer words. Confirms the catalog's second-position primary and the always-strong penult behind its even-length clash cells, for Ute (syllable-counting).
